blocks.label: Overview
blocks.title: What is motion graphics, and when does a brand need it?

paras: Motion graphics is animated design: type, shapes, illustration and data brought to life over time. Unlike filmed video it does not need a location, a cast or a shoot day, which makes it the practical choice when what you need to show is an idea rather than a place.

It earns its place in a few specific situations. When something is hard to explain in a sentence — a process, a product's mechanism, a service with several steps — motion can show the sequence instead of describing it. When a brand needs consistency at volume, a motion system produces dozens of on-brand pieces from the same templates. And when a post needs to survive the scroll, movement in the first second is what buys the next five.

Filmed video does things motion cannot: real people, real places, real products in hand. Most brands need both, which is why we produce and edit both rather than pushing every brief toward the format we prefer.

items: Brands whose social video gets skipped — the content is fine, the first second is not.
Companies with something complicated to explain — software, fintech, logistics, healthcare, industrial products.

items.q: What affects the cost of a video?
a: Mostly: length, whether it is animated or filmed, how much original design or illustration it needs, whether there is a shoot with a crew and location, voice-over, licensed music, and how many language and platform versions you need.

An animated explainer built from existing brand assets and a filmed brand film with a crew are different orders of work. We scope from the brief rather than quoting a fixed rate per minute, because a minute of simple animation and a minute of filmed production are not comparable.

items.q: Do you do animation, filming, or both?
a: Both, and often in the same project. Many of the most effective pieces combine filmed footage with motion graphics — real product or people, with animated type and graphics carrying the explanation.

items.q: Can you work with footage we already have?
a: Yes, and it is frequently the fastest route to something useful. Plenty of companies have paid for shoots that were never edited properly. Editing existing footage, adding motion and versioning it per platform often produces more than commissioning a new shoot.

Yes — Arabic and English, including Arabic voice-over and subtitles. Arabic on screen needs its own attention: right-to-left type, timing that suits Arabic reading pace, and layouts designed for it rather than an English layout with the text swapped.

items.q: How long does a video take?
a: It depends on length, complexity and whether filming is involved. The stage that most often decides the timeline is approval on script and style frames — once those are settled, production is predictable. We agree the schedule against those milestones rather than a single delivery date.

items.q: Can motion graphics work for a small brand?
a: Yes, and usually better than a big production would. A defined motion system with reusable templates lets a small brand publish consistent video every week, which does more over a year than one expensive film. That system is part of branding and design.
